headline: High risk of prompt-injection and cascading errors from ctx’s browser/MCP context flowing into a writable, networked RAG agent; compliance exposure is also plausible.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ctx can observe Claude Code PostToolUse/Stop events and uses MCP stdio, while the course agent reads/writes files and runs shell commands. That creates a plausible content bridge where attacker-controlled outputs from A can be consumed by B as trusted instructions. The interaction is documented only indirectly, so uncertainty pushes to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF ctx observes tool output that B later parses as instructions or prompts, injection is possible.
IF B ingests files or stdin/stdout from the same workspace without provenance checks, malicious content can steer tool use.
mitigations: Add a provenance tag to all A→B handoffs.
Require B to treat A output as untrusted text only.
Disable automatic parsing of tool logs as prompts.
Use separate workspaces for A and B.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and allowlist filters at the bridge.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches audit/runtime logs, graph data, and MCP servers; B touches configuration secrets and academic data, and can read/write the filesystem. A shared local environment can leak sensitive artifacts between them even without explicit network exfiltration. Because the shared workspace is not stated but filesystem overlap is plausible, the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF A and B share a filesystem or mounted workspace, files can be exposed across agents.
IF B reads logs or notebooks produced by A, sensitive runtime data may be copied into B outputs.
mitigations: Separate A and B into distinct directories.
Restrict B read access to only required inputs.
Rotate or redact secrets before any file handoff.
Review logs for secrets before sharing.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A supports multiple instances and uses filesystem/filesystem-adjacent MCP hooks; B can write the filesystem and execute shell commands. Even though B cannot modify git state, overlapping writes to shared files or logs can still race and corrupt outputs. The conflict is real in default local development setups, so medium fits better than low.
conditions: IF A and B write to the same directory, file clobbering or inconsistent state can occur.
IF multiple instances of either agent run concurrently, shared artifacts may race.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Serialize writes with a lock file.
Disable concurrent runs during shared edits.
Snapshot shared state before execution.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is a context-management agent that observes tool events, and B is a LangGraph-based RAG/course agent that can act on retrieved content and shell outputs. If B treats A’s summaries or logs as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream actions or generated answers. Because the pair lacks explicit verification boundaries, the default path is dangerous enough for high.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated summaries as ground truth, mistakes propagate into later steps.
IF B triggers API calls or shell actions from unverified A output, downstream errors amplify.
mitigations: Require human review before action-taking.
Insert a verification step between A and B.
Mark A outputs as advisory only.
Log source provenance alongside every claim.
requires-engineering: add schema validation for A→B handoffs.

E_compliance.rationale: A touches audit/runtime logs and graph data, while B handles configuration secrets and academic papers in a local development environment. That combination can create retention and residency mismatches if logs or secrets are copied into shared artifacts. The profiles do not show a direct residency violation, so medium is the cautious fit; A is cited for its data classes and B for secret handling.
conditions: IF secrets or logs are retained in shared notebooks or exports, retention policy mismatch occurs.
IF EU or regulated data is routed through the local dev environment without controls, compliance obligations may be breached.
mitigations: Minimize retained logs.
Redact secrets before export.
Keep regulated data out of shared notebooks.
Document retention for each agent.
requires-engineering: add policy-based data-loss controls.
